claims.text: A hybrid framework combining refractory-element MLIPs with an elemental-melting-point-variance correction will accurately predict melting temperatures and entropies of fusion for refractory high-entropy alloys.
WTaMoNbV has substantial diversity in the melting points and densities of its constituent elements.
The target refractory high-entropy alloys have sparse experimental thermodynamic data.
The proposed workflow trains an MLIP on solid- and liquid-phase AIMD data, applies two-phase coexistence simulations, and adds a correction based on elemental melting-point variance.
Experimental data are unavailable in the relevant high-temperature regime above 2000 K.
Liquid-phase short-range order and local-environment fluctuations are poorly captured by classical potentials and are critical to accurate entropy-of-fusion calculations.
Lennard-Jones potentials do not provide reliable predictions for multicomponent high-entropy alloys.
Lennard-Jones potentials fail because they cannot represent the complex electronic interactions of multicomponent alloys.
CALPHAD predictions become unreliable for understudied alloys and high temperatures when their thermodynamic databases are incomplete or inaccurate.
The proposed MLIP will capture the many-body interactions and short-range-order evolution governing the liquid structure.
A correction based on elemental melting-point variance accounts for kinetic and thermodynamic barriers caused by disparate elemental melting points.
The hybrid framework will predict melting temperatures within 5% of experimental values.
The framework will provide reliable entropy-of-fusion estimates for experimentally untested compositions.
Existing high-throughput predictions have narrow composition-domain validity.
A single interatomic potential cannot reliably generalize across diverse refractory-alloy systems.
The proposed method is valid for substitutional solid-solution alloys.
The method may fail for oxides, carbides, and other systems with very large heats of formation because high-entropy theory does not strictly apply to them.
Highly positive mixing enthalpies can provide a precipitation-driving force that overcomes the stabilizing effect of configurational entropy.
Interatomic-potential transferability at extreme temperatures is uncertain when complex precipitate behavior occurs.
Transferability may also fail for amorphous phases or when the training data do not cover the liquid configurational space of multicomponent combinations.
